articles.title: Lift-off! NASA launches Roman Space Telescope to tackle dark-energy mysteries
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 August 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02727-7The space observatory will have an expansive view of the Universe as well as sharp resolution.
articles.content:
The field of view of the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope (artist’s illustration) will be roughly 100 times bigger than that of the Hubble Space Telescope. Credit: NASA/Handout via Reuters

The largest infrared digital camera ever built and its scientific companion, a massive mirror originally designed for a spy satellite, are now safely in orbit, after the flawless launch of NASA’s newest flagship telescope. The US$4.3-billion Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope lifted off atop a SpaceX rocket at 7:35 a.m. local time today from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, and it will soon be on its way to its final location.

The observatory is expected to yield a wealth of discoveries, from insight into the nature of ‘dark energy’, the force causing the Universe’s expansion, to millions of stars in the Milky Way and the planets that orbit them. It is named after Nancy Grace Roman (1925–2018), NASA’s first chief astronomer and a leading figure in many of the agency’s most impactful scientific programmes, including the Hubble Space Telescope.

The Roman telescope is the final member of a trio of complementary sky-mapping observatories. It is joining the US-led Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile, which was inaugurated in 2025, and Euclid, a space telescope launched by the European Space Agency in 2023 (see ‘Complementary skills’). Together, these observatories are expected to change the face of astronomy, with unprecedented amounts of data and immense, astoundingly detailed images.

Complementary skills The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope has a bigger primary mirror than the Euclid telescope. It also has keener vision, which can be measured using a property called angular resolution with the unit arcseconds: the lower the number, the higher the resolution. Euclid has a bigger field of view, which is often measured in square degrees and describes how much of the sky a telescope sees. Nancy Grace Roman wide-field instrument Euclid visible camera Mirror diameter 2.4 metres (primary mirror) 1.2 metres Angular resolution 0.11 arcseconds per pixel 0.18 arcseconds Field of view 0.28 square degrees 0.57 square degree

Between the three sky-surveying projects, Roman’s unique capability is taking frequent, deep images in the infrared — the part of the light spectrum that consists of wavelengths slightly too long to be seen by the human eye — with its 300-megapixel camera (see ‘Wide eye on the Universe’). “It’s going to be revolutionary,” says Tony Tyson, a physicist at the University of California, Davis.

Into the infrared

Roman’s infrared vision is key: the light from the Universe’s most distant objects is transformed into longer, ‘redder’ wavelengths by billions of years of cosmic expansion. But most infrared light is blocked by Earth’s atmosphere. This means that for infrared astronomy, space is the place to be.

Roman’s sensitivity to infrared light means that it will be able to peer into the Universe’s deep past and observe highly reddened galaxies that are difficult for Rubin or Euclid to see, says Rachel Mandelbaum, an astrophysicist at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. Mapping the Universe’s galaxies in 3D, as Roman will do, enables cosmologists to reconstruct the expansion history of the Universe (see ‘Wide eye on the Universe’).

Moreover, Roman will be an engine for spotting thousands of distant supernova explosions, which cosmologists can use as signposts to measure how the rate of cosmic expansion has varied over the aeons. This will help researchers to understand whether the push of dark energy has been uniform — or has changed over space and time.

Closer to home, the telescope will map an unprecedented 20 billion stars in the Milky Way, including many inside and beyond the galaxy’s dusty central region, says Dominic Benford, an astrophysicist at NASA in Washington DC who is the programme scientist on the Roman project. Dust blocks more visible light than infrared radiation. Thanks to Roman’s talent for infrared imagery, “we can see through the galaxy like no other mission before”, Benford says.

The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), which NASA launched at the end of 2021, is also mainly an infrared observatory. But the field of view of Roman’s main instrument can cover the entire Moon, whereas JWST’s takes in an area 100 times smaller. Typically, Roman will make the first discovery of events such as supernovae, and astronomers will then follow up with detailed studies with JWST, as well as with other observatories.

Long road to L2

The first concept for the telescope that would eventually become Roman began with the surprising discovery in the 1990s that the Universe’s rate of expansion is accelerating, not slowing down, thanks to dark energy. One of the researchers leading that discovery was Saul Perlmutter at the Lawerence Berkeley National Laboratory in California, who analysed the traits of a few dozen supernovae that formed in the last 7 billion years. Perlmutter and Michael Levi, a physicist also at the Lawrence Berkeley laboratory, proposed a satellite called the Supernova Acceleration Probe (SNAP) that would be able to investigate even older supernovae. This would allow for more precise measurement of dark energy’s effects.

Under the new name of WFIRST, the project received a boost in 2012 when the secretive US National Reconnaissance Office called NASA to offer two free half-built space telescopes, each with a 2.4 metre primary mirror — about as large as the one on the Hubble Space Telescope. NASA ended up adopting one of the orphaned mirrors after realizing that its wide-field capabilities, which had been designed to be pointed towards Earth originally, were just what was needed for the dark-energy mission.

This represents a major scientific breakthrough with broad significance for astronomy and cosmology, promising large-scale benefits to humanity's knowledge of the universe.
articles.personality_title: NASA launches Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope to explore the universe’s mysteries
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists want to understand dark energy, a force that makes the universe expand faster. To do this, they need powerful telescopes that can see far into space and capture detailed images, especially in infrared light, which is mostly blocked by Earth’s atmosphere.

**What happened** – On August 30, 2026, NASA successfully launched the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope from Florida. This new space telescope has the largest infrared digital camera ever built and a big mirror originally made for a spy satellite. It will join two other major telescopes, the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile and the European Space Agency’s Euclid telescope, to study the universe together.

**Impact** – The Roman Telescope can take wide, sharp pictures in infrared light, allowing it to see very distant galaxies and stars hidden by cosmic dust. It will map 20 billion stars in our Milky Way and observe thousands of supernova explosions, which help scientists measure how dark energy affects the universe’s growth over time. Its wide view is much larger than the James Webb Space Telescope’s, making it perfect for finding new cosmic events.

**What’s next step** – The telescope will travel to a special spot in space called L2, where it can observe the sky without Earth’s interference. Scientists will use its data to better understand dark energy, the history of the universe’s expansion, and the structure of our galaxy. It will also work with other telescopes to study exciting discoveries in more detail.

**One-sentence takeaway** – NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will provide powerful new views of the universe in infrared light, helping scientists unravel the mysteries of dark energy and our galaxy’s stars.
articles.personality_title_fr: NASA lance le télescope spatial Nancy Grace Roman pour explorer les mystères de l’univers
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les scientifiques cherchent à comprendre l’énergie sombre, une force qui accélère l’expansion de l’univers. Pour cela, ils ont besoin de télescopes puissants capables de voir très loin dans l’espace et de capturer des images détaillées, notamment en lumière infrarouge, qui est en grande partie bloquée par l’atmosphère terrestre.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Le 30 août 2026, la NASA a lancé avec succès le télescope spatial Nancy Grace Roman depuis la Floride. Ce nouveau télescope spatial possède la plus grande caméra numérique infrarouge jamais construite et un grand miroir initialement conçu pour un satellite espion. Il rejoint deux autres grands télescopes, l’observatoire Vera C. Rubin au Chili et le télescope Euclid de l’Agence spatiale européenne, pour étudier l’univers ensemble.

**Impact** – Le télescope Roman peut prendre des images larges et précises en lumière infrarouge, ce qui lui permet de voir des galaxies très lointaines et des étoiles cachées par la poussière cosmique. Il cartographiera 20 milliards d’étoiles dans notre Voie lactée et observera des milliers d’explosions de supernovae, qui aident les scientifiques à mesurer comment l’énergie sombre influence la croissance de l’univers au fil du temps. Son champ de vision est beaucoup plus grand que celui du télescope spatial James Webb, ce qui le rend idéal pour découvrir de nouveaux événements cosmiques.

**Prochaine étape** – Le télescope se rendra à un point spécial dans l’espace appelé L2, où il pourra observer le ciel sans être gêné par la Terre. Les scientifiques utiliseront ses données pour mieux comprendre l’énergie sombre, l’histoire de l’expansion de l’univers et la structure de notre galaxie. Il collaborera aussi avec d’autres télescopes pour étudier plus en détail les découvertes passionnantes.

**En résumé** – Le télescope spatial Nancy Grace Roman de la NASA offrira de nouvelles vues puissantes de l’univers en lumière infrarouge, aidant les scientifiques à percer les mystères de l’énergie sombre et des étoiles de notre galaxie.
articles.personality_title_es: NASA lanza el telescopio espacial Nancy Grace Roman para explorar los misterios del universo
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los científicos quieren entender la energía oscura, una fuerza que hace que el universo se expanda más rápido. Para ello, necesitan telescopios potentes que puedan ver muy lejos y capturar imágenes detalladas, especialmente en luz infrarroja, que la atmósfera de la Tierra bloquea en gran medida.

**Qué pasó** – El 30 de agosto de 2026, la NASA lanzó con éxito el telescopio espacial Nancy Grace Roman desde Florida. Este nuevo telescopio tiene la cámara digital infrarroja más grande jamás construida y un gran espejo originalmente hecho para un satélite espía. Se unirá a dos otros telescopios importantes, el Observatorio Vera C. Rubin en Chile y el telescopio Euclid de la Agencia Espacial Europea, para estudiar el universo juntos.

**Impacto** – El telescopio Roman puede tomar imágenes amplias y nítidas en luz infrarroja, lo que le permite ver galaxias muy lejanas y estrellas ocultas por polvo cósmico. Mapeará 20 mil millones de estrellas en nuestra Vía Láctea y observará miles de explosiones de supernovas, que ayudan a los científicos a medir cómo la energía oscura afecta el crecimiento del universo con el tiempo. Su campo de visión es mucho más grande que el del telescopio espacial James Webb, haciéndolo ideal para encontrar nuevos eventos cósmicos.

**Próximo paso** – El telescopio viajará a un lugar especial en el espacio llamado L2, donde podrá observar el cielo sin interferencia de la Tierra. Los científicos usarán sus datos para entender mejor la energía oscura, la historia de la expansión del universo y la estructura de nuestra galaxia. También trabajará con otros telescopios para estudiar más a fondo los descubrimientos emocionantes.

**Conclusión en una frase** – El telescopio espacial Nancy Grace Roman de la NASA ofrecerá nuevas y poderosas vistas del universo en luz infrarroja, ayudando a los científicos a descubrir los misterios de la energía oscura y las estrellas de nuestra galaxia.

articles.title: NASA Welcomes Türkiye as Newest Artemis Accords Signatory
articles.summary: During a ceremony hosted by NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman at the agency’s headquarters in Washington on Monday, the Republic of Türkiye signed the Artemis Accords, joining the growing international coalition of like-minded nations dedicated to peaceful, transparent space exploration. “It is my privilege to welcome the Republic of Türkiye as the 71st signatory of the […]
articles.content:
Turkish Minister of Industry and Technology, Mehmet Fatih Kacır, 3rd from left, signs the Artemis Accords for the Republic of Türkiye as NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, left, U.S. Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Space and Environment Connor Tomlinson, and Turkish Space Agency President, Yusuf Kıraç, right, look on, Monday, August 31, 2026, at the Mary W. Jackson NASA Headquarters building in Washington. NASA/Bill Ingalls

During a ceremony hosted by NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman at the agency’s headquarters in Washington on Monday, the Republic of Türkiye signed the Artemis Accords, joining the growing international coalition of like-minded nations dedicated to peaceful, transparent space exploration.

“It is my privilege to welcome the Republic of Türkiye as the 71st signatory of the Artemis Accords,” said Isaacman. “Last year, President Trump directed NASA to accelerate its return to the lunar surface and establish humanity’s first enduring presence on another world, a Moon Base, as well as lay the foundation for the manned exploration of Mars. NASA never undertakes these grand endeavors alone. On the Moon Base, we’re taking the Artemis Accords principles and putting them into practice on the lunar surface. NASA has invited every signatory to take part in this endeavor, creating opportunities for nations to contribute major pieces of hardware, scientific payloads, technology demonstrations, CubeSats, and other capabilities to future Artemis missions.”

Turkish Minister of Industry and Technology Mehmet Fatih Kacır signed on behalf of Türkiye. The President of the Turkish Space Agency Yusuf Kıraç, and the U.S. Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Space and Environment Connor Tomlinson, also participated in the event.

Türkiye’s recent achievements in human spaceflight underscore its commitment to space exploration. In 2024, the country’s first astronaut, Alper Gezervaci, traveled to the International Space Station on Axiom Mission 3 and conducted scientific research alongside NASA astronauts. That same year, a second Turkish astronaut, Tuva Atasever, flew on Virgin Galactic 07 suborbital mission, conducting experiments and physiology research.

Türkiye will soon launch its first lunar mission, AYAP-1, joining the small but growing group of countries building and launching their own satellites to the Moon.

The country’s signing also comes as the country prepares to host the International Astronautical Congress in Antalya this October. Dozens of Artemis Accords signatories are expected to attend to discuss the future of peaceful and transparent space exploration.

In 2020, NASA and the State Department joined with seven other founding nations to establish the Artemis Accords, responding to the growing interest in lunar activities by both governments and private companies. They introduced the first set of practical principles aimed at enhancing the safety and coordination between nations as they explore the Moon, Mars, and beyond, committing nations to:

explore peaceably and transparently

render aid to those in need

enable access to scientific data

ensure activities do not interfere with those of others

preserve historically significant sites and artifacts by developing best practices

By signing the Artemis Accords, nations open the door to opportunities for future lunar exploration with NASA, advancing humanity’s return to the Moon, and shaping the Golden Age of space exploration and innovation.

Learn more about the Artemis Accords at:

https://www.nasa.gov/artemis-accords

-end-

articles.personality_title: Türkiye joins Artemis Accords to boost peaceful space exploration
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The Artemis Accords are agreements between countries that guide how nations explore space peacefully and openly. They were created by NASA and other countries in 2020 to help countries work together on missions to the Moon, Mars, and beyond.

**What happened** – On August 31, 2026, Türkiye officially signed the Artemis Accords at NASA’s headquarters in Washington. Turkish Minister of Industry and Technology Mehmet Fatih Kacır signed the agreement, with NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman and other officials present. This made Türkiye the 71st country to join the group.

**Impact** – Türkiye’s signing is important because it shows the country’s growing role in space exploration. Türkiye has already sent two astronauts to space and is preparing its first mission to the Moon, called AYAP-1. By joining the Accords, Türkiye can work closely with NASA and other countries on future space missions, sharing technology and research.

**What’s next step** – Türkiye will participate in upcoming Artemis missions, which aim to build a permanent Moon Base. The country will also host the International Astronautical Congress in October 2026, where many Artemis Accords members will meet to discuss peaceful space exploration.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Türkiye’s joining of the Artemis Accords marks a key step in global teamwork for exploring the Moon and beyond in a peaceful and open way.
articles.personality_title_fr: La Turquie rejoint les accords Artemis pour renforcer l’exploration spatiale pacifique
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les accords Artemis sont des ententes entre pays qui guident l’exploration spatiale de manière pacifique et transparente. Ils ont été créés par la NASA et d’autres pays en 2020 pour faciliter la coopération lors des missions vers la Lune, Mars et au-delà.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Le 31 août 2026, la Turquie a officiellement signé les accords Artemis au siège de la NASA à Washington. Le ministre turc de l’Industrie et de la Technologie, Mehmet Fatih Kacır, a signé l’accord en présence du directeur de la NASA, Jared Isaacman, et d’autres responsables. La Turquie est devenue le 71e pays à rejoindre ce groupe.

**Impact** – La signature de la Turquie est importante car elle montre le rôle croissant du pays dans l’exploration spatiale. La Turquie a déjà envoyé deux astronautes dans l’espace et prépare sa première mission lunaire, appelée AYAP-1. En rejoignant les accords, la Turquie peut collaborer étroitement avec la NASA et d’autres pays sur les futures missions spatiales, en partageant technologies et recherches.

**Prochaine étape** – La Turquie participera aux prochaines missions Artemis, qui visent à construire une base permanente sur la Lune. Le pays accueillera aussi le Congrès international d’astronautique en octobre 2026, où plusieurs membres des accords Artemis se réuniront pour discuter de l’exploration spatiale pacifique.

**Résumé en une phrase** – L’adhésion de la Turquie aux accords Artemis marque une étape clé pour la coopération mondiale dans l’exploration pacifique et ouverte de la Lune et au-delà.
articles.personality_title_es: Turquía se une a los Acuerdos Artemis para impulsar la exploración espacial pacífica
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los Acuerdos Artemis son acuerdos entre países que guían cómo explorar el espacio de forma pacífica y transparente. Fueron creados por la NASA y otros países en 2020 para ayudar a colaborar en misiones a la Luna, Marte y más allá.

**Qué pasó** – El 31 de agosto de 2026, Turquía firmó oficialmente los Acuerdos Artemis en la sede de la NASA en Washington. El Ministro de Industria y Tecnología de Turquía, Mehmet Fatih Kacır, firmó el acuerdo, acompañado por el administrador de la NASA, Jared Isaacman, y otros funcionarios. Turquía se convirtió en el país número 71 en unirse.

**Impacto** – La firma de Turquía es importante porque muestra el creciente papel del país en la exploración espacial. Turquía ya ha enviado dos astronautas al espacio y prepara su primera misión lunar, llamada AYAP-1. Al unirse a los Acuerdos, Turquía podrá colaborar estrechamente con la NASA y otros países en futuras misiones, compartiendo tecnología e investigación.

**Próximo paso** – Turquía participará en las próximas misiones Artemis, que buscan construir una base permanente en la Luna. También será sede del Congreso Internacional de Astronáutica en octubre de 2026, donde muchos miembros de los Acuerdos Artemis se reunirán para hablar sobre la exploración espacial pacífica.

**Resumen en una frase** – La adhesión de Turquía a los Acuerdos Artemis marca un paso importante para el trabajo conjunto global en la exploración pacífica y abierta de la Luna y más allá.
